messages.body_plain:
Hello,

So, as I said before, I´m not experienced in R, so I would appreciate if you could give me some advice on the integration of MDArray and Renjin from the point of view of functionality and interface.

So, let´s say I have an MDArray (or MDMatrix) and I can convert that to a R Matrix as described in the previous email.  Now, should I create an RMatrix class and add methods to this class?  Then I would probably need also a RDataSet class and other such R classes.

Another approach would be to create a Renjin class and then "import" the MDArray to Renjin and from them on work inside Renjin sending to it strings to be interpreted.  I don´t really like this approach as the integration is very "thin".

On the other hand, I also think that if we start with a data set in Renjin, how to make use of MDArray features?

One of the things I´ve read many times is that programming in R is a real pain, so could MDArray/Renjin come up with a better model that allowed for programming in Ruby and geting all of R´s functionality?  For instance, it would be great if I could start with a large multidimensional array (in a NetCDF file), make a loop (in Ruby) that took views from this array, for each of those views find, say, a linear regression with Renjin, and the store the results in a Ruby array for printing and visualization.

Thanks for comments/advice.

Cheers,

Rodrigo

Then you can reference enunciate version 1.29-SNAPSHOT and it should treat Renjin's classes correctly.

HTH

Alex

messages.subject: Re: GPLv3 => ASL, MIT, Mozilla, BSD license?
messages.subject_clean: GPLv3 => ASL, MIT, Mozilla, BSD license?
messages.body_plain:
I think the issue is more nuanced than the mechanics of class-file linking. Although I'm not a lawyer, my understanding is that it comes down to the extent you can make the argument that your software and Renjin remain two substantively different, independent works.

First, I hasten to remark that the GPL doesn't have to confer any obligations on your *users*: they can download your product and Renjin and do whatever they like with it; They have no obligations as GPL licensees unless they want to distribute Renjin outside their organization.

As far as your own obligations go, I fear that the answer is "it depends" :

>From the GNU FAQ:
http://www.gnu.org/licenses/gpl-faq.html#GPLInProprietarySystem

> I'd like to incorporate GPL-covered software in my proprietary system. Can I do this?
> "[...] in many cases you can distribute the GPL-covered software alongside your proprietary system. To do this validly, you must make sure that the free and non-free programs communicate at arms length, that they are not combined in a way that would make them effectively a single program.
>
> If the two programs remain well separated, like the compiler and the kernel, or like an editor and a shell, then you can treat them as two separate programs—but you have to do it properly. The issue is simply one of form: how you describe what you are doing."

My read of that is that the spirit of the integration is key. If someone used Renjin as the basis for a proprietary, general purpose data analysis package I'd be pretty annoyed, regardless of how the programs communicate.

If you've got a specialized commercial package for fisheries analysis or high frequency trading or whatever and you want to offer integration with Renjin as as separate add-on so your users can interact with your software using the R language, I presume you could make the argument that your product is a separate work.

One example of this is icCube, a commercial BI server that offers integration with Renjin as a separate download.
http://www.iccube.com/support/documentation/mdx_integration/r_integration.html

If you're looking to be very cautious, you could restrict yourself to using the javax.script API or offer a separate download.

If you find a good lawyer (someone has to be a lawyer, right?) to confirm/contradict my reasoned opinion, please let me know!

Best,
Alex

messages.subject: Re: Packages
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jonathan,

this is a very good question, because install.packages() is specific to GNU R and therefore doesn't work in Renjin. If you try and load a CRAN package using the library() function, Renjin will look for that package in our public repository. You can see the build state of CRAN packages against Renjin at http://packages.renjin.org. If you start Renjin from the command line and type 'library(exptest)' you will see Maven fetching the package and Renjin will attach it to the search path. You therefore do not need to "install" the package, but you do need an internet connection. If you go to the page for this specific package (http://packages.renjin.org/packages/exptest.html) you will find how to add it as a dependency in Maven. Note that many CRAN packages will not work in Renjin because the build failed. Some packages will load, but may not fully work because a dependency is missing. The exptest package happens to be a small -pure R- package with no dependencies ;-)

We are currently in the process of completely revising the documentation for Renjin. One of the topics will be how to create, load and share packages targeted at Renjin. Packaging will be based on using Maven, but there are some design decisions to be made regarding the use of fully qualified names in packages. We're very exited about some of the things we have cooked up for the next release and we hope to be able to announce its availability soon.

Regards,

Maarten-Jan

messages.body_plain:
My storage is a one dimensional java array in ROW-major order! Now, how can I do it?  If the array is created in Renjin and exported to MDArray then I could probably convert indexes, but can I send a row-major array to Renjin?

Thanks,

Rodrigo

Em terça-feira, 29 de abril de 2014 06h03min48s UTC-3, Alexander Bertram escreveu:

> Sounds great!
>
> Renjin has a layer of abstraction between R code and data storage, so you could easily expose your MDArray as an R object.
>
> If your underlying storage is indeed a one dimensional java array, in column-major order, then it is as simple as:
>
> AttributeMap attributes = AttributeMap.builder().setDim(numRows, numCols).build();
> DoubleVector matrix = DoubleArrayVector.unsafe(myArray, attributes);
>
> If you have more than two dimensions, use :
> int dim[] = {3, 5, 9, 4 };  //etc
> AttributeMap attributes = AttributeMap.builder().setDim(new IntVector(dim)).build();
>
> If the array is very large, you can use the unsafe() factory method to create the DoubleVector without creating a copy of the array. But you have to guarantee that the matrix won't change, as Renjin assumes that it can lazily defer operations on large vectors.
>
> You can also provide your own DoubleVector implementation, for sparse matrices, for example, where you can organize the underlying storage as you need. The DistanceMatrix object is a good example of this:
>
> https://github.com/bedatadriven/renjin/blob/master/core/src/main/java/org/renjin/DistanceMatrix.java
>
> I should also note that in principle referencing a 2TB matrix using a DoubleVector facade over a NetCDF file should be no problem, as Renjin will defer operations on large data objects until usually a reduce operation like sum() or mean(), but there are still some basic operations for which still aren't set up to defer operations properly, and they might try to create a copy of your 2TB matrix, which will fail. For example, this *will* work:
>
> x <- mMdArrayJavaClass$readCdf("2tbmatrix.dat")
> y <- t(x / 2)
> print(dim(y))
> print(y[3000,4000])
>
> because y just contains a basically a wrapper that says: when someone asks for element i,j, grab j,i from x and divide by two.
>
> however, I don't believe rbind() is set up to defer operations, so
>
> z <- rbind(x, x)
>
> will probably try to allocate a java array of 4tb, which won't succeed.
>
> Also, vectors in Renjin are currently limited by 32-bit (actually 31-bit) indices, so the total logical size of a matrix is limited. We need to think a bit about the best way to do this: GNU R has introduced 64-bit indices, but R itself still only has 64-bit floating point numbers and 32-bit signed integers, so you still can't fully address the large vectors, at least from R code.
>
> I think what might be interesting for Renjin is just to make the R "integer" type a 64-bit signed integer, and then 64-bit indices follow naturally, but I'm not sure what impact if any this will have on performance.
>
> Anyway, if you hit any obstacles, let me know and I'll see what we can do quickly to eliminate the bottleneck.
>
> Best,
> Alex

messages.body_plain:
Hi Andy,
Those packages are built with the renjin-maven-plugin, the only thing we do is generate a POM file based on the DESCRIPTION file:

See for example:
http://nexus.bedatadriven.com/content/groups/public/org/renjin/cran/KernSmooth/2.23-8-SNAPSHOT/KernSmooth-2.23-8-20130217.125415-1.pom

I haven't looked yet at testthat, but I suspect the issue is with Renjin's support for the S4 type system. The code is there: most of the S4 system is actually written in R, and we've implemented the handful of "native" hooks that this code expects, but I think there are some complexities surrounding packages and S4 that I've missed.

Generally -- I think we might be better off pulling the whole of the S4 type system out of "user space" and into the interpreter itself. It is of course very meta to implement in a language's type system in that language itself, but my sense is that it has enormous costs in turns of complexity, and also lost opportunities for optimization as the interpreter doesn't have any special knowledge about S4 classes/methods.

But if you can find a few quick fixes to get S4 packages running that would be obviously be well worth the time in the near time!

Best,
Alex

messages.subject: Re: Method isFinite
messages.body_plain:
Hi Rodrigo,

Yes, this is correct, or rather, this is the only way for these two particular java methods to behave.

If you evaluate  is.na <http://is.na>(as.double(NA_integer_)) in Renjin, it will give you what you expect (TRUE)

The behavior you're describing is that of the JVM - which doesn't know anything about NA values for integers. Both Renjin and GNU R introduce the idea of NA for integers by reserving one of the 32 bits for the NA flag. In practice, this means that at the lowest level, IntVector.NA =  -2147483648

When you call DoubleVector.isFinite(double), the JVM will implicitly cast  -2147483648 to  -2147483648.0. But of course, for 64-bit double values, we use the NaN bit + the signaling payload to represent NA. The JVM doesn't have any way of knowing that  -2147483648.0 should map to NA (Nor would want it to randomly convert -2^31 to NA either!)

This is logic that we have to implement ourselves. So you can use IntVector.isNA(x) instead of DoubleVector.isNA() as NA is the only non-finite value in the R integer domain.

HTH,

Alex
